title: Moral beauty
hookLine: seeing great goodness gives a warm lift psychologists call elevation (Haidt)

lines: SNOW, A SHOVEL, NO ONE ASKED.
cards: Snow overnight. At six in the morning a teenager from down the street is already out with a shovel, clearing the driveway of the elderly woman next door. No one asked.
No one is filming. He finishes, leans the shovel by her steps, and walks home.
Some people who see a moment like that describe a warmth spreading in the chest, a lump in the throat, a sudden wish to go and do something good themselves.
That reaction has a name, and a psychologist went looking for it.

teach.h: MORAL BEAUTY: GOODNESS IN A DEED.
teach.b: The psychologist is Jonathan Haidt, and the name he gave it is elevation. First, what it is. Elevation is the response to seeing someone act with unusual goodness: kindness, courage, generosity, forgiveness.
Haidt calls that goodness moral beauty: beauty in a deed instead of a sunset. Second, what it feels like, as people describe it.
A warm or glowing feeling in the chest. Sometimes tears. A sense of being lifted, opened.
Haidt set it beside disgust as its opposite: disgust is the feeling of watching people sink below the ordinary, and elevation the feeling of watching someone rise above it. Third, what it does.

teach.h: IT MAKES PEOPLE WANT TO HELP.
teach.b: In Haidt's research, people who felt elevation reported wanting to help others and to become better people themselves. Goodness, seen, seems to be catching.
In Haidt's account the feeling points outward, toward other people and toward the person the watcher would like to be. Fourth, an old teacher who knew this.
Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who wrote private notes to himself, kept a habit of thinking about the good in the people around him.

teach.h: THINK OF THE VIRTUES OF THOSE WHO LIVE WITH THEE.
teach.b: In George Long's translation: "When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee." He didn't call it elevation.

He used it as medicine: when he wanted delight, he went looking for someone's goodness on purpose. Moral beauty doesn't need a headline. It turns up on ordinary streets, in small doses, for anyone watching for it.

how: Some people deliberately seek out stories of great kindness, or recall the virtues of people they know, as a way to lift themselves and to prompt their own good deeds; Marcus Aurelius describes doing this in his Meditations.

o: following every rule exactly, so no one can find fault with you
unusual goodness seen in a person's deed, which can lift the watcher
a pleasing face that people assume belongs to a good person

p: the warm lift of seeing it
think of the virtues of others

s: elevation is just a warm feeling that stays inside
in Haidt's research it points outward: people report wanting to help and to become better.
Haidt set elevation beside disgust as its opposite
disgust at people sinking below the ordinary; elevation at someone rising above it.
Marcus Aurelius called this feeling elevation
he didn't use that word. he used it as medicine: thinking of the virtues of those around him.

games.q: you've just watched a stranger do something quietly, unusually kind. according to Haidt's research, what do people in your place often report wanting?
o: to help others and be better themselves.
to feel worse about their own lives.
to find out what the stranger wanted.
games.why: elevation tends to be catching: people who feel it report wanting to help and to become better people.

practice: Bring to mind one great kindness you've seen, read about or received, and go to the moment itself: the hands, the faces, what was said.
Stay with it for a few breaths and notice whether anything moves in your chest or your throat, and whether it asks anything of you. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Moral beauty. Unusual goodness, seen in a person's deed. Seeing it, some people describe a warm lift that Jonathan Haidt calls elevation. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: elevation. A good deed can lift the one who only watched it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Haidt, J., 'Elevation and the positive psychology of morality', in Flourishing (2003); The Happiness Hypothesis, chapter 9
